players.product: Mozaic HAMR nearline HDDs (44TB Mozaic 4+ -> 50TB Mozaic 5) for AI mass-capacity storage

quarterly_data.signal: DECEMBER QUARTER (FISCAL Q2 2026) SET COMPANY RECORDS: CEO Dave Mosley said the quarter set new company records for exabyte shipments, gross margin, operating margin and non-GAAP EPS, with sequential revenue growth across nearly all end markets. CFO Gianluca Romano: revenue came in at $2.83 billion, up 7% sequentially and up 22% year-over-year; non-GAAP gross margin was 42.2%, up 210 basis points sequentially, helped by the pricing strategy and a richer mix of high-capacity drives as HAMR shipments ramp; non-GAAP operating margin was 31.9%; non-GAAP EPS was $3.11, up 19% quarter-over-quarter. Seagate shipped 190 exabytes, up 26% year-over-year, 'while keeping overall unit capacity relatively flat'. Free cash flow was $607 million, the highest level in 8 years, and Seagate retired approximately $500 million of exchangeable senior notes due 2028, leaving gross debt of approximately $4.5 billion. CEO Dave Mosley: for calendar 2025, revenue rose by over 25% and gross margins improved by nearly 740 basis points.
quarterly_data.figure: revenue $2.83 billion (up 22% year-over-year); non-GAAP gross margin 42.2%; non-GAAP EPS $3.11; 190 exabytes (up 26% year-over-year); free cash flow $607 million

quarterly_data.signal: DATA CENTER CARRIES THE QUARTER AND CAPACITY PER DRIVE KEEPS RISING: the data center market accounted for 87% of shipment volume. Seagate shipped 165 exabytes into data center, up 4% sequentially and 31% year-on-year, and data center revenue was $2.2 billion, up 5% sequentially and 28% year-on-year, on demand from global cloud customers and sequential growth across enterprise OEM markets (CFO Gianluca Romano). Average nearline drive capacity rose 22% year-over-year, 'approaching 23 terabytes per drive' (CEO Dave Mosley). Average cloud nearline capacity increased to nearly 26 terabytes and 'will continue to grow with the ramp of HAMR-based Mozaic products'. Revenue per terabyte stayed relatively stable. In enterprise OEM, demand for storage servers is increasing, 'driven in large part by the adoption of AI applications and need to store data at an enterprise edge'. Edge IoT made up the remaining 21% of revenue at $601 million.
quarterly_data.figure: data center 87% of our shipment volume; 165 exabytes (31% year-on-year); data center revenue $2.2 billion (28% year-on-year); average cloud nearline capacity nearly 26 terabytes; edge IoT $601 million

quarterly_data.signal: NEARLINE SOLD OUT FOR CALENDAR 2026; CALENDAR 2027 VOLUMES AGREED BUT NOT YET PRICED (as of January 2026): 'Our nearline capacity is fully allocated through calendar year 2026, and we expect to begin accepting orders for the first half of calendar year 2027 in the coming months' (CEO Dave Mosley). Demand visibility is improving because of 'long-term agreements in place with major cloud customers through calendar '27'. Multiple cloud customers are already discussing demand growth projections for calendar '28, and 'supply assurance remains their highest priority'. CFO Gianluca Romano: for calendar 2026 'we have PO in place for all the quarters, so volume and pricing is well defined' and 'the vast, vast majority of the volume is already allocated'; any extra output in a quarter is sold on the open market. For calendar '27 Seagate has 'very good indication and agreement on volumes', but the price is not fixed yet. Seagate has not started the longest-lead-time parts for '27 but will very soon. Seagate will meet demand through supply discipline, growing exabytes through areal density 'without increasing unit production volume'. Manufacturing is running 'quite, quite tight', and customers who cannot get supply now are planning data center procurement further ahead.
quarterly_data.figure: nearline capacity fully allocated through calendar year 2026; long-term agreements with major cloud customers through calendar '27; calendar '28 demand projections under discussion

quarterly_data.signal: HAMR (MOZAIC 3) BECOMES THE VOLUME PLATFORM: by year-end, quarterly HAMR shipments had exceeded 1.5 million units and kept ramping (CEO Dave Mosley). Mozaic 3 is now qualified with all major U.S. CSP customers and remains on track to be qualified at all global CSPs within the first half of calendar 2026. HAMR drives have been running in cloud production environments 'for more than 3 quarters now'. CFO Gianluca Romano: 'We qualified the last big cloud service provider in the U.S. and we have qualified 6 out of 8 of the top cloud service providers'. Another customer qualified on HAMR lets Seagate ramp a little more HAMR volume in the March quarter, which helps margin. Seagate deliberately limited 3 terabyte per platter output because its factories were full and it was moving to the 4 terabyte per platter product.
quarterly_data.figure: quarterly HAMR shipments exceeded 1.5 million units; qualified 6 out of 8 of the top cloud service providers

quarterly_data.signal: NEXT HAMR STEP, MOZAIC 4 (4 TERABYTE PER DISK, 40 TERABYTES PER DRIVE), STARTS TO RAMP (as of January 2026): qualifications of the second-generation Mozaic 4 products are 'progressing well'. Seagate expects to begin the Mozaic 4 ramp 'later this quarter' (the March quarter) and to have multiple CSPs qualified in the coming months (CEO Dave Mosley). CFO Gianluca Romano: Seagate is qualifying 2 major customers on the new product. Finishing qualification and ramping those customers probably runs through the end of the calendar year, with a strong impact in the next calendar year. Unit costs stay fairly similar while content per unit rises, so high-volume 40 terabyte drives should bring 'a fairly important reduction in cost per terabyte compared to the current HAMR'. Management plans to move to the 4 terabyte per platter product 'very aggressively'. The ramp will still be 'fairly prescriptive', because manufacturing is tight and products already in the pipeline are committed to customers. The plan is a big transition to 4 terabytes per platter over the coming few years, followed by 5 terabytes per platter. Roadmap: 7 terabytes per disk has been demonstrated in the lab, and the areal density road map extends to 10 terabytes per disk, expected early in the next decade. Management said it is 'on the plan or slightly ahead' of its node-transition timelines.
quarterly_data.figure: Mozaic 4: 4 terabyte per disk to 40 terabytes per drive; qualifying 2 major customers; 7 terabytes per disk demonstrated in lab; road map to 10 terabytes per disk

quarterly_data.signal: PRICING POWER AND INCREMENTAL MARGIN ABOVE THE INVESTOR-DAY MODEL (as of January 2026): CFO Gianluca Romano said Seagate is executing 'a little bit better than what we discussed at our Investor Day, where we presented a model with a 50% incremental margin above $2.6 billion of revenue', and has done better every quarter. The pricing strategy and a richer high-capacity mix together lifted revenue per terabyte modestly quarter over quarter, a trend expected to continue into the March quarter. The mix shift helps cost reduction, supply-demand conditions support pricing, and both are expected to lift gross margin through the calendar year. CEO Dave Mosley: pricing 'will be dictated by the demand'. As each long-term agreement rolls into the next year and customers move to new, supply-constrained products, Seagate sets pricing based on demand: 'I think flat to slightly up is certainly possible'. Management said no offshoring or change in manufacturing strategy is behind the margin gains, and the systems business is 'fairly small scale in comparison'.
quarterly_data.figure: 50% incremental margin above $2.6 billion of revenue (Investor Day model), done better every quarter; pricing flat to slightly up is certainly possible

quarterly_data.signal: MARCH-QUARTER (FISCAL Q3 2026) GUIDANCE (CFO Gianluca Romano): revenue in the range of $2.9 billion, plus or minus $100 million, a 34% year-over-year improvement at the midpoint. Non-GAAP operating expenses of approximately $290 million, non-GAAP operating margin approaching the mid-30% range, and non-GAAP EPS of $3.40 plus or minus $0.20, on a tax rate of about 16% and a non-GAAP diluted share count of 230 million shares. Data center demand, particularly from global cloud customers, is expected to more than offset typical March-quarter seasonality in edge IoT, and the guide includes a further HAMR ramp. Seagate expects 'sequential improvement to both the top and bottom line throughout calendar 2026', and operating expenses should reach the 10%-of-revenue target in the March quarter.
quarterly_data.figure: revenue $2.9 billion, plus or minus $100 million (34% year-over-year at midpoint); non-GAAP EPS $3.40 plus or minus $0.20

quarterly_data.signal: CAPEX STAYS AT THE LOW END OF THE 4%-6% RANGE WHILE FUNDING THE HAMR RAMP: Seagate invested $116 million in capital expenditures in the December quarter, roughly 4% of revenue, and expects fiscal year 2026 capex inside its target range of 4% to 6% of revenue, 'supporting our HAMR transition and HAMR ramp' (CFO Gianluca Romano). CEO Dave Mosley: Seagate will probably stay well within the 4% to 6% range, spending a little more as revenue rises, with maintenance tools as the first priority. Depreciation follows capex on a 10 years useful life. Wafer-fab lead times are long, so Seagate starts wafers based on what it knows it can deliver 6 to 9 months later, which is one reason it plans about a year at a time inside its LTAs. Management plans to reinvest in itself to keep pushing areal density.
quarterly_data.figure: $116 million capex in December quarter (roughly 4% of revenue); fiscal year 2026 capex inside 4% to 6% of revenue

quarterly_data.signal: AI DEMAND DRIVERS AND THE HDD STORAGE TIER (CEO Dave Mosley): video keeps driving hard-drive demand. Platforms like YouTube see 20 million video uploads daily, up from just 2 million 3 years ago, and that does not yet include the full surge expected from AI-driven video applications. Agentic AI 'relies on persistent access to large volumes of historic data'. Hard drives anchor the mass-capacity tier, storing the checkpoint data sets used for training and supporting the vector databases that give inference its context. On the warm tier, random small-block workloads are 'probably memory', while big data is 'a little bit of memory on the front end and a lot of hard drive on the back end'. The architectural tier that stores large data such as checkpoints, physical AI and video 'will probably remain constant for the next decade'. Hard drives are not idle background storage: 'They're working 24/7', optimized largely for streaming performance.
